title: White musicians and the French opera orchestra turnover
summary: Few white men aspired to be performers, but opera musicians stayed on as teachers and dance promoters.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: you see, in the early, oh in the 1820s and the 1830s and 40s, families tended to discourage a man who thought of taking up the piano or something, although they would have a genius like Gottschall, of course he left New Orleans when he was 10 or 11 years old to study for all the next years in France, the 1860s until he came back. But very few white men in New Orleans aspire to become, say, a performer in the orchestra of the French theater. But what happened to keep a lot of white musicians around and even growing in number, was a kind of reverse process. Every three or four years there had to be a heavy infusion of new blood into the French orchestra. For two reasons, either some who had been here two or three years wanted to return to Germany, or to France, to wherever they were from, Italy. And others liked it here and it drifted into other ways of making a living. Most often musicals are closely associated with it. For instance, they might become choir masters, they might become private teachers, they might get involved in promoting the dance halls, or there were myriad ways that they could sort of drift out of the opera, but remain here, adopt the city, and they were always enthusiastic musicians. They made a widening musical circle, and this thing continued through all those years. About every two or three years, either a complete new orchestra or at least a whole lot of new musicians came from abroad.
